title: The interior castle
hook: Teresa of Ávila pictured the soul as a castle of many rooms, with God at the center

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius and the road to Bethlehem. Your line was step into the scene. Did you build somebody's room for a moment before you answered them? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

How do you walk into a house you already live in? A Spanish nun named Teresa of Ávila asked a question like that, and she admitted it sounded like nonsense. She'd been asked by her superiors to write about prayer for the sisters in her convents, and she wasn't sure where to start. So she asked God for help, and, she says, a picture came to her. A castle. Not a castle out on a hill somewhere, but one inside every person. Full of rooms. And the strange thing, as she tells it, is that plenty of souls stay out in the courtyard and never go in. Today's word is her picture.
screen: `A HOUSE YOU ALREADY LIVE IN.` → `A PICTURE CAME TO HER.` → `LIVING IN THE COURTYARD.`

segments.voice: Teresa's book is called The Interior Castle, and she builds it on a line of Jesus from John's Gospel: "In my Father's house are many mansions." Here's the castle, turned four ways. First, what it's made of. She says to think of the soul as a castle made of a single diamond, or of very clear crystal, with many rooms. She divides the book into seven dwelling places, and she says each has many rooms of its own. In the very center is the main room, where God lives, and where, she says, the most secret things pass between God and the soul. Second, the door. If the soul is the castle, how do you get in? Teresa's answer: the door is prayer and reflection. People who never pray, she says, stay outside in the courtyard, among the snakes and creatures of the outer wall, busy with everything except the castle itself. Third, the layout. Don't imagine the rooms in a straight row, she tells her sisters, like a hallway. Think of a palmetto, a plant with many layers wrapped around a tender center you have to peel your way toward. The journey in isn't a march. It's more like unwrapping. Fourth, the room you never leave. Teresa says the room of self-knowledge matters in every stage, even for someone far inside. Knowing yourself honestly, with your faults, she says, keeps a person humble, however far in they've come. Notice where she puts God. Not far off, at the end of a long road, but at the center of the person, waiting to be visited. The rooms are the way there.
screen: `A CASTLE OF DIAMOND, WITH GOD AT THE CENTER.` · `THE DOOR IS PRAYER.` · `NOT A HALLWAY: A PALMETTO.` · `THE ROOM OF SELF-KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE ARE MANY MANSIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture your inner rooms. Sit comfortably and let your breathing settle. Notice the courtyard first, the noise near the outer wall: today's errands, messages, worries. Don't fight them. Just see that they're out there. Then step through a door. Notice one quieter room, maybe a memory, or someone you love. Then one more, a little further in. If you pray, you can rest at the threshold of the center and say nothing. If not, simply notice how it feels to be further in than the courtyard. The bell holds the time.
The interior castle. Teresa of Ávila's picture of the soul: a castle of clear crystal with many rooms, God at the center, and prayer as the door. Today's word.

Your line: many rooms. Today, when you're stuck in the courtyard, rushing and reacting, pause at a doorway, any real doorway, and take one breath one room further in. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholics and other Christians read The Interior Castle as a guide to growth in prayer, often with a spiritual director; Carmelite communities, the order Teresa reformed, study it closely.

ask God for help, and use the picture that comes.
refuse until a priest writes it instead.

what a scholar hears: seven dwelling places, each with many rooms, built on John 14:2, with self-knowledge needed at every stage.

notes: All Interior Castle material is paraphrased. Confirm: Teresa writing at her superiors' request; asking the Lord for help before the image came; the castle of a single diamond or very clear crystal (I.1.1); the link to John 14:2; the door as prayer and reflection (I.1.7); snakes and creatures in the outer court; the palmetto image (I.2.8); self-knowledge needed at every stage and humility as the bread for every meal (I.2.8–9). Confirm the 'nonsense' remark about entering a castle one is already in (I.1.5).
'Seven dwelling places' is stated because the book itself is divided into seven; confirm.
howItsDone names Carmelites and Teresa's reform of the order; confirm wording. No dates given (the index's 1577 left out).

Editor: cut 'humility is the bread that goes with every meal'. In Teresa the bread image is usually attached to self-knowledge, not humility, and its exact place (Interior Castle I.2 or Life 13) could not be verified; the line now says only that honest self-knowledge keeps a person humble at every stage.
